metadata.title: Maine SLD: evidence and instruction-need practice
metadata.purpose: Practice connecting evidence to the current Maine SLD form and explaining a supported provisional recommendation. This activity does not determine an actual child's eligibility.
metadata.caseDesignReview: Reviewed each case against the current posted Maine SLD form/checklist. Samira now uses the complete fictional source record, edition 1.0.0, and matching worked key shared with the PDF worksheet, covering Q1-Q9 and documented interpretation limits. Other cases retain their stated evidence and training assumptions. Not an independent specialist validation; original score fixtures are preserved.

disclosures: Alex and Jordan are fictional cases. All scores, dates, benchmark values and intervention history are simulated training examples.
Composite/index scores are independently stipulated for discussion, not calculated from the listed subtests or publisher scoring software.
No percentile ranks, confidence intervals, raw/process scores, significance tests or diagnostic cutoffs are supplied or inferred.
This fictional battery is not a required universal battery. Secondary/complementary WISC-V tests, Alphabet Writing Fluency and Orthographic Choice are not included.
No copyrighted test items or secured manual content are included; public test names and score structures are used.
Use the current official form, full evaluation record and team discussion for actual decisions. No separate adverse-effect form is required for SLD.
More evidence needed is a permitted training response, not an additional official form option. The activity must not automatically grade evidence selection or produce a real eligibility verdict.
Marisol and Taylor are additional original fictional practice cases. Their facts and Taylor’s generic achievement scores are simulated; no real student record is included.

Marisol’s standardized score record is intentionally not supplied because this excerpt does not establish the linguistic suitability and interpretation limits of the assessment summary. This is not a blanket prohibition on standardized assessment of multilingual learners.

Taylor’s four generic age-based standard scores are separate from Alex’s WISC-V/WIAT-4 fixture. The full-record training assumptions establish the practice conclusion; isolated scores or passing grades do not automatically determine eligibility.

Samira and Avery are original fictional cases. Supplemental observations, student/family statements, teaching logs and classroom-task counts in all cases are invented training evidence, not actual records or validated diagnostic measures.

Case details distinguish reported or observed evidence, stipulated full-record findings and unresolved questions. Stipulated findings let participants practice later decisions; they are not proved by the short excerpts alone.

Participants may choose a case by grade, academic focus or context. The facts within a case belong together; changing a language, schooling or instruction premise requires reexamining the evidence and conclusions, not simply replacing a demographic label.

Samira uses the complete fictional S1-S9 record and matching facilitator key shared with the PDF worksheet; Marisol retains unresolved evidence. Multilingual status predicts neither outcome. Classroom-task counts describe the stated task and support conditions only and are not standard scores, norms or eligibility thresholds.

formSteps.label: Q1: achievement
formSteps.prompt: Do multiple valid and reliable sources show adequate achievement for age AND meeting State-approved grade-level standards in ALL eight academic areas?

routes.feedback: Document supporting evidence and go to Q8; this pathway does not support SLD qualification.
Identify affected areas, document verification and continue to Q2.

formSteps.feedback: A YES requires evidence across all eight areas for both age and grade standards. One score, passing grades or promotion alone does not establish that premise.

formSteps.label: Q2: appropriate instruction
formSteps.prompt: If achievement is inadequate, is the underachievement due to lack of learning experiences and instruction appropriate for age or State-approved grade-level standards?

routes.feedback: Document verification and go to Q8; inadequate appropriate instruction does not support SLD qualification under this form.
Document appropriate opportunity to learn and continue to Q3.

formSteps.feedback: YES here identifies instruction as the explanation for underachievement. Review actual methodologies, delivery by qualified personnel, attendance, access and culturally/linguistically appropriate instruction.

formSteps.label: Q3: primary causes
formSteps.prompt: Is the lack of achievement primarily the result of any listed factor? Record a separate YES or NO and supporting verification for each subpart; the practice summary does not replace those four determinations.

subparts.label: Environmental, cultural or economic disadvantage and/or limited English proficiency

routes.feedback: Any YES directs the team to Q8 and no SLD qualification under this form.
All NO responses direct the team to Q4.

formSteps.feedback: Determine primary cause, not the mere presence of a coexisting factor. Every subpart needs supporting evidence; multilingual status alone neither establishes nor excludes SLD.

formSteps.label: Q4: relevant pattern
formSteps.prompt: Using appropriate assessments, does the IEP team find a pattern of strengths and weaknesses in performance, achievement or both that is relevant to SLD identification, relative to age, State-approved grade-level standards or intellectual development? Document strengths AND weaknesses for each of the four evidence streams. Psychological-processing documentation includes standardized measures and composite scores as specified by the form; do not substitute classroom observations for that evidence.

routes.feedback: Document the relevant pattern and continue to Q5.
Proceed to Q8; this pathway does not support SLD qualification.

formSteps.feedback: Examine convergence and inconsistencies across the four evidence categories. A low processing score alone does not determine relevance or SLD. Findings based on shared subtests are not independent replications.

formSteps.label: Q5: observation narrative
formSteps.prompt: Describe relevant behavior during observation and its relationship to academic functioning in the area of difficulty.

routes.feedback: Record observed behavior and its academic relationship, then continue to Q6.

formSteps.feedback: Q5 is a narrative field. Use appropriate learning-environment/classroom observation evidence and follow applicable observation and consent procedures.

formSteps.label: Q6: medical findings narrative
formSteps.prompt: Record educationally relevant medical findings, including when no relevant finding is reported.

routes.feedback: Record relevant findings, then continue to Q7.

formSteps.feedback: Q6 is a narrative field. A medical diagnosis alone neither establishes SLD nor replaces the educational evaluation.

formSteps.label: Q7: validity / qualifications
formSteps.prompt: Are the evaluations used valid and reliable assessments and performed by qualified individuals?
formSteps.feedback: If NO, the form requests assessment-specific information about validity, reliability or evaluator qualifications. Missing documentation alone is not proof an assessment was invalid. The form does not print an automatic stopping or bypass rule at Q7.
formSteps.guidance: Review validity, reliability and evaluator qualifications. If NO, identify each affected assessment and explain its validity, reliability or qualification concern. The form gives no automatic Q7 stop/bypass branch. Interpretation guidance: resolve concerns or obtain appropriate alternative evidence before relying on results for Q8.

formSteps.label: Q8: SLD conclusion
formSteps.prompt: Does a specific learning disability exist?

routes.feedback: YES proceeds to the separate special-education need decision at Q9.
NO means no SLD qualification under this form; address other suspected needs and appropriate support as warranted.

formSteps.feedback: Record the supported team conclusion. Identifying SLD at Q8 does not by itself establish that special education is required at Q9.

formSteps.label: Q9: instruction needed
formSteps.prompt: If SLD exists, does the child require special education and related services (9a), or can the need be adequately addressed through general education interventions and/or accommodations (9b)? Summarize the basis.

options.label: 9a: special education and related services required
9b: general education adequately addresses the need

routes.feedback: 9a supports SLD special-education eligibility when the complete record establishes the need.
9b does not support SLD special-education eligibility on the stated facts, even if Q8 is YES.

formSteps.feedback: The official form has options a and b and requires a summary. More evidence needed is an accepted training response, not a third official checkbox. Explain impact, general education sufficiency and any necessary adaptation to content, methodology or delivery. Individualization, program, staff or placement alone does not define SDI. A Section 504 decision remains separate.

cases.title: Alex, Grade 4: evidence and instruction need

evidenceSupplement.title: Reported: student and family perspective
evidenceSupplement.text: Alex enjoys designing marble runs and explaining how they work. In the fictional interview, Alex says it is easier to explain a story than to read it aloud and asks to preview directions privately. Family describes shared reading and says homework directions often require adult reading; this is help with access, not evidence of low motivation or limited family support.

evidenceSupplement.title: Observed: reading and content access
evidenceSupplement.text: In a 20-minute classroom observation, Alex independently reads a Grade 4 science paragraph, pauses repeatedly at unfamiliar words and loses the place twice. On five teacher-created content questions Alex answers two after independent reading and four after listening to a parallel passage of comparable content difficulty. Different passages and the audio support limit direct comparison. The observation suggests an access difference; it is not a controlled experiment or a standardized comprehension score.

evidenceSupplement.title: Documented in the fictional log: intervention delivery
evidenceSupplement.text: The reading specialist's 12-week log records 44 of 48 planned 30-minute sessions, taught in a group of three using explicit sound-symbol instruction, blending, cumulative word practice and connected-text reading. Four sessions were missed because of school scheduling. Five weekly-probe summaries at baseline and weeks 3, 6, 9 and 12 are 54, 56, 58, 60 and 61 correct words per minute on alternate passages at the same monitoring level. The separate 110 benchmark is a stipulated classroom comparison, not an eligibility cutoff. Three fidelity observations document the planned lesson components; parent updates summarize progress at weeks 4, 8 and 12.

evidenceSupplement.title: Unresolved: instruction required after the evaluation
evidenceSupplement.text: The excerpt does not include a completed comparison of what general education can adequately provide, the precise disability-related teaching adaptations Alex needs, or independent transfer into unpracticed classroom reading. Participants should identify which records and team members could clarify those issues. Twelve weeks describes this case and does not prescribe a waiting period or a prerequisite for evaluation.

narrative: Alex is age 9, in Grade 4, English-dominant, with 96% attendance. Appropriate core instruction and 12 weeks of explicit decoding intervention (4 x 30 minutes weekly) have documented implementation. Reading increases from 54 to 61 correct words per minute; the fictional grade benchmark is 110.

With audio text, Alex answers grade-level content questions independently. Independent reading stays slow with decoding errors despite extra time. Family reports that Alex discusses stories heard aloud but needs help reading homework directions.

Assume valid testing by qualified evaluators, a documented review finding no primary exclusionary cause, normal vision/hearing screening, and no educationally relevant medical finding. The full score record is simulated for discussion; original reporting and scoring detail remain intentional verification gaps.

evidenceSupplement.title: Counterfactual premise: complete instruction-need review
evidenceSupplement.text: This is an explicitly stipulated counterfactual for practicing the distinction between Q8 and Q9. Participants should identify the independent-performance, implementation, maintenance and access evidence needed before using 9b in a real case. A general education setting or a widely used strategy alone does not settle the distinction.

cases.title: Jordan, Grade 5: achievement and family concerns
cases.selectionLabel: Jordan, Grade 5: classroom and family evidence
cases.languageContext: English used at home and school; assessment access reviewed in the stipulated evaluation

evidenceSupplement.title: Stipulated and illustrated: academic evidence
evidenceSupplement.text: The complete evaluation establishes adequate age-based achievement and independent grade-level work across all eight areas. Illustrative work includes accurate independent unfamiliar-word reading, a written explanation with a clear claim and supporting details, and independently solved grade-level multistep mathematics. Separate classroom discussion and listening tasks inform oral expression and listening comprehension. These examples illustrate the premise; they are not a replacement for the full eight-area record.

evidenceSupplement.title: Reported and observed: different task settings
evidenceSupplement.text: Family's two-week homework log records repeated requests to repeat directions and frustration when several assignments are announced together. Jordan says a single written list helps and wants homework to take less of the evening. In class, the observer notes that Jordan checks posted directions and completes the academic work independently; posted directions do not provide answers or adult academic prompting. The team should explore workload, task organization and setting differences without dismissing the family report.

evidenceSupplement.title: Unresolved: support for the reported difficulty
evidenceSupplement.text: The low working-memory result is one source to interpret alongside daily functioning. Its specific cause and the need for other evaluation are not established by this excerpt. Plan a family-agreed trial of written directions and a short follow-up log documenting time, prompts and frustration while considering any other suspected disability. The SLD pathway conclusion is limited to the stipulated academic evidence.

narrative: Jordan is age 10. The family reports homework frustration and difficulty remembering multistep directions. For this exercise, assume a valid, comprehensive evaluation using appropriate achievement assessments, classroom measures, representative work and teacher/family information.

The team reviews all eight academic areas. Multiple sources show adequate achievement for age AND meeting grade-level standards independently in every area. One valid working-memory measure gives a standard score of 78.

cases.title: Marisol, Grade 4: multilingual access and evidence gaps

evidenceSupplement.title: Reported: language choices and student priorities
evidenceSupplement.text: Marisol says she likes to sketch an explanation before writing and wants to read science books with her classmates. Family prefers Spanish for evaluation meetings and wants the team to preserve both languages. The interpreter-supported interview distinguishes conversational Spanish, school-taught Spanish literacy and developing English academic language; none is assumed from nationality, a surname or everyday conversation alone.

evidenceSupplement.title: Observed: supports and task demands
evidenceSupplement.text: On two science activities, the teacher records accurate concept explanations using a labeled diagram and partner rehearsal. Without those supports, written explanations omit sequence words and details. During unfamiliar-word reading, Marisol guesses from initial letters even when the word's meaning has been explained. The tasks show both language demands and a word-reading concern; they cannot separate their causes. The brief Spanish sample remains descriptive, with schooling and text difficulty needing review.

evidenceSupplement.title: Documentation limit: unresolved form decisions
evidenceSupplement.text: This excerpt does not support a completed Q1 determination. Later Q2-Q7 discussion entries are evidence-planning notes, not a verified progression through the official form. Q8 remains unresolved and neither Q9 option is reached. More evidence needed is a training status, not an official checkbox; lack of supplied validity documentation does not itself prove that an assessment is invalid.

evidenceSupplement.title: Actionable gaps: source and purpose
evidenceSupplement.text: The ESOL teacher will document language use and development by domain plus actual access supports. With family permission, the case manager will seek earlier curriculum and attendance records and ask what literacy was explicitly taught. The evaluator and qualified bilingual personnel will plan appropriate language/literacy tasks and record adaptations and limits. Classroom staff will collect matched work samples with task, language, instruction and support conditions identified. These are evidence requests while evaluation and support proceed, not extra prerequisites before referral.

cases.practiceFocus: Language access, assessment validity and an evidence plan
cases.languageContext: Spanish and English; language and literacy history require further review
narrative: Marisol is age 9 years, 10 months, in Grade 4. She uses Spanish with her family and English and Spanish at school. Her family describes detailed Spanish storytelling, an interest in science and persistent difficulty reading unfamiliar words in Spanish. She explains mathematical reasoning well with diagrams. She attended Spanish-medium school in Grades 1-2, with a four-month interruption during a school closure, and entered English-medium instruction in Grade 3. Prior literacy-instruction records are incomplete.

The current school documents regular attendance and scheduled ESOL instruction. The ESOL teacher reports stronger English listening and discussion with visual/context support than independent academic reading and written explanations. English development differs across tasks and domains. The language-access plan is available, but classroom implementation logs and the earlier school's instruction and intervention records have not yet been reviewed. These gaps do not establish whether inadequate instruction primarily explains the reading concern.

During an English science lesson, Marisol explains the concept using a diagram and partner discussion, but has difficulty independently reading the written directions. In a brief Spanish reading sample arranged by qualified bilingual staff, she hesitates on unfamiliar words; no age/grade comparison, systematic response-to-teaching record or comprehensive Spanish literacy assessment accompanies that sample. Her family requests an evaluation and participation through a qualified Spanish interpreter. The team has begun the evaluation process while language and reading supports continue.

An English-only assessment summary lists low reading performance but does not document the assessment's linguistic suitability, norming applicability, administration adaptations or interpretation limits. No standardized scores from that summary are supplied for this practice record. Vision/hearing screening reports, the complete medical history and a full review across the academic areas are also absent from the excerpt. The record raises a reading concern and an assessment-validity question; it establishes neither SLD nor a language-only explanation.
assumptions: All details are fictional. Schooling durations, service schedules and language descriptions are case context, not eligibility thresholds or required waiting periods.
The evaluation proceeds with appropriate procedures while ESOL, content-access and reading supports continue; Marisol does not have to reach an English-proficiency threshold before evaluation.

The English-only summary's suitability has not been established. Its omission from this score record is a validity safeguard, not a finding that all English assessments or all standardized assessments are unsuitable for multilingual learners.

The abbreviated record intentionally leaves appropriate-instruction verification, primary-cause analysis, assessment validity, SLD identification and any necessary special-education instruction unresolved. Family concerns and strengths remain relevant.

This does not mean all standardized assessments are unsuitable for multilingual learners.

Use the child's native language or communication mode unless clearly infeasible. Appropriate work/performance evidence is needed where relevant norms are unavailable; converting a score format does not repair validity.

Q8.responseLabel: SLD conclusion unresolved in this practice excerpt
Q8.feedback: Complete the appropriate evaluation and instruction/primary-cause review before making the supported team conclusion. Uncertainty calls for timely evidence gathering, not a language-proficiency waiting rule or an automatic SLD or language-only verdict.

Q9.feedback: Q9 follows a supported Q8 YES conclusion. This planning exercise does not settle that premise or whether general education can adequately meet the need. Identify necessary supports and evidence to investigate; if eligible, ESOL and special education can both be provided.

cases.title: Taylor, Grade 5: progress and the instruction it requires

evidenceSupplement.title: Documented in the fictional log: progress and transfer
evidenceSupplement.text: Over the last instructional cycle, Taylor attends 38 of 40 planned lessons. narrative: Taylor is age 10 years, 7 months, in Grade 5 and receives reading instruction under an IEP. A comprehensive reevaluation includes appropriate achievement and psychological-processing assessments, repeated progress measures, classroom observations, work samples and student/family input. The qualified evaluators document a relevant pattern across the required evidence streams and continuing SLD affecting basic reading and reading fluency. Appropriate core instruction, intervention implementation and a documented review of each primary-cause factor are verified.

Taylor contributes thoughtful ideas to class discussion and meets many science and social-studies assignment expectations with accessible audio/text, previewed vocabulary and extra reading time. Independent unfamiliar-word reading and connected-text fluency remain below age and Grade 5 expectations across valid assessment, classroom work and repeated reading measures. Successful supported content work does not show adequate independent achievement in every academic area.

Taylor's progress measures show improvement during explicitly sequenced decoding instruction: smaller teaching steps, carefully selected word patterns, cumulative practice, immediate corrective feedback and flexible pacing adjusted from ongoing error analysis. Implementation and longitudinal transfer records document that these adaptations address Taylor's disability-related learning needs. Appropriate general education interventions and accommodations have not adequately addressed those needs without the specified teaching adaptations. The full reevaluation establishes that the adaptations remain necessary for access to and progress in the curriculum.

The family asks whether better report-card grades mean that the reading instruction can end. The team has not withdrawn necessary instruction to test that idea. It reviews existing instruction, implementation, independent performance, supported performance and generalization data. No educationally relevant medical finding is reported in the complete reviewed record. evidenceSupplement.title: S1: Referral, consent, participation and source record
evidenceSupplement.text:
Coordinator Morgan Ellis's record, September 30: at intervention planning on April 3, 2026, Rania received interpreted information about the performance data to be collected, general-education services, strategies for increasing learning and her right to request an evaluation; this information was reviewed again August 20. The family and Grade 4 teacher requested evaluation August 20 for persistent word-reading difficulty. Prior notices and the evaluation plan were explained with qualified Arabic interpretation; written parent consent was received August 24. Evaluation activities occurred September 4-30. The new regular-classroom observation in S7 followed consent. Instruction and ESOL continued; no additional intervention cycle was required before evaluation.

The October 2 meeting notice was provided September 18; Rania confirmed attendance and requested interpretation. Reports and an interpreted review were provided September 30. Proposed participants are Rania; Melanie Voss, general educator; Nina Park, special educator; Morgan Ellis, district representative; Dr. Elena Mercer, school psychologist able to interpret evaluation results; Hana Nasser, ESOL teacher; and Dalia Mansour, qualified Arabic interpreter/language consultant. evidenceSupplement.title: S2: Language, literacy, student and family evidence
evidenceSupplement.text:
Hana Nasser, Maine-certified ESOL teacher, and Dalia Mansour, qualified Arabic-English language consultant, interviewed Samira and Rania on September 11. Samira has heard and used Levantine Arabic from birth and English since preschool at age 4. She has attended this English-medium school continuously since kindergarten in fall 2022. Arabic and English are both used at home; the family describes detailed, sequenced Arabic stories and age-appropriate everyday conversations. A 45-minute weekly community class since September 2024 provides introductory Modern Standard Arabic print instruction. Samira reads some taught Arabic words, but this exposure is not equivalent to her English literacy instruction; no Arabic-English reading-score comparison is made.

The simulated February 2026 Grade 3 ACCESS Online report gives the domain proficiency-level scores below. These are English-proficiency results, not disability or achievement scores. WIDA's 2025-2026 reset means scale scores cannot be compared with prior years; the 2026 proficiency-level scores also require caution because they use the prior cut scores. No overall score is computed here. The team uses the snapshot with classroom evidence, not as an exit rule or a waiting period for evaluation.

Comparable oral-language samples with familiar content, pictures and the same 0-12 local rubric improved from 7/12 in September 2025 to 10/12 in September 2026: more complete explanations, causal vocabulary and clarification of misunderstandings. In September Samira correctly explained 18/20 familiar spoken word meanings but independently read only 9/20 different printed words using the same taught spelling patterns. Directions and vocabulary were checked before local decoding tasks. The word-reading errors persisted on familiar English vocabulary, including sounds shared across her languages; neither this check nor bilingual status by itself identifies a disability.

Rania reports stable housing, food access, predictable caregiving and regular access to school materials, with no schooling interruption or chronic disruption during the reviewed period. She values Arabic use and wants interpreted progress updates. Samira wants to read her science-display captions independently. The school does not treat family income, language, culture or limited formal Arabic literacy as an explanation without evidence.

evidenceSupplement.title: S3: Appropriate instruction, delivery and repeated progress
evidenceSupplement.text:
Teacher/interventionist records reviewed September 28 document qualified, Maine-certified teachers, 97% attendance across the reviewed school period, and daily 90-minute English literacy instruction. Core teaching included explicit phonemic analysis, cumulative phonics/word analysis, spelling, supported oral reading, vocabulary and comprehension, with modeling, guided practice and correction. ESOL was 30 minutes four days weekly; visual directions, clarified vocabulary, oral rehearsal and content-language support were available daily. These methods addressed the English literacy skills assessed here; attendance alone was not used to establish instructional adequacy.

Reading specialist Nina Park delivered a research-based explicit decoding/fluency intervention in addition to core instruction. The methods used sound-letter analysis, word-part decoding and supported connected-text reading, drawing on the WWC foundational-skills and Grades 4-9 intervention guides listed below; this does not imply that the fictional local program itself has been validated. Four 25-minute sessions were planned weekly across nine instructional weeks April 6-June 12 (excluding spring break) and five instructional weeks August 24-September 25. Of 56 planned sessions, 51 occurred: 34/36 in spring and 17/20 in fall. Two absences and three school-event cancellations account for five missed sessions. No school intervention was delivered during summer; voluntary home materials were not counted as sessions. These are 14 instructional weeks, not 14 uninterrupted calendar weeks.

Checks by the literacy coach on April 17, May 15, August 28 and September 18 documented respectively 9/10, 10/10, 9/10 and 10/10 planned lesson elements: explicit modeling, guided practice, immediate feedback and cumulative review. Hana verified access to directions and task vocabulary at each review. The last two weeks included the instructional comparison in S8. The broad monitoring probes below remained independent, unpracticed and at the same difficulty; narrow taught-item gains in S8 do not replace them.

At each review date below, Rania received the results and explanation through a qualified Arabic interpreter. Review notes recorded her questions and the next instructional adjustment. The word-list and fluency data were not withheld until the eligibility meeting.

evidenceSupplement.text:
Melanie Voss and the curriculum coordinator reviewed June 2026 Grade 3 core-curriculum summative results, September 2026 beginning-Grade-4 assessments and classroom work. Tasks were mapped to Maine's grade-level ELA/mathematics expectations and taught prerequisites, with ordinary language-access supports recorded. Local minimums below are instructional criteria, not eligibility cutoffs or nationally validated norms.

Achievement norm-group comparability for an English nationally normed achievement battery was not established for this Arabic-English literacy history. Consistent with the form's conditional instruction, the Q1 evidence therefore uses the multi-tiered performance record, work samples and district summative assessments; no standardized achievement score is used. No age/grade-equivalent conversion is available or invented. Q4c may use district core-curriculum summative evidence, not only nationally normed tests.

All reading-comprehension scores below involved Samira reading the printed text herself, with her own rereading and no adult reading, audio or word supply. Untimed comprehension and slow/inaccurate reading can coexist. Oral presentation is separately identified for listening and mathematics tasks so it is not misrepresented as reading performance. evidenceSupplement.title: S5: Psychological processing and cognitive assessment report
evidenceSupplement.text:
Dr. Elena Mercer, Maine-credentialed school psychologist trained in these instruments and culturally responsive assessment, administered selected WISC-V subtests on September 16 and CTOPP-2 on September 17. All subtests required for the listed composites were administered and scored according to the manuals in English; no items or directions were informally translated during standardized administration. English task directions and response demands were understood, and ordinary permitted practice items were completed. The language consultant helped review history and interpretation, not translate standardized test items.

Scores below are fictional age-based composite/index standard scores (mean 100, SD 15). WISC-V NVI is not an FSIQ; the indexes overlap in contributing subtests and are not independent replications. No IQ-achievement discrepancy, significance calculation or score cutoff is used. The report did not identify globally depressed reasoning, visual-spatial or processing-speed performance; English phonological-awareness and rapid-symbolic-naming tasks were more difficult than phonological-memory tasks.

These national norms are not asserted to represent Samira's exact Arabic-English experience. Reduced verbal demand is not culture-free assessment. WISC-V results provide a bounded description of performance on the selected tasks; CTOPP-2 results describe English phonological task performance, not a language-independent deficit or its cause. The evaluator used them as contributing evidence, checked against language history, familiar-vocabulary tasks, instruction and independent classroom errors. English schooling and understood directions support access but do not themselves eliminate normative bias. The report does not use a low English composite alone to identify disability.

evidenceSupplement.title: S6: Health, sensory/motor, developmental, adaptive and emotional review
evidenceSupplement.text:
These findings come from distinct sources, not a single blanket exclusion statement. The team must consider whether a factor primarily accounts for underachievement, not merely whether a characteristic or concern exists. Family/context and language evidence for this review is in S2; instructional opportunity is in S3.

School nurse Marina Cole, RN, reviewed the school health record, parent health questionnaire and available pediatric summary with consent on September 10. No reported seizures, traumatic brain injury, diagnosed ADHD, significant sleep problem, chronic illness, medication effect or other educationally relevant medical finding was identified in the reviewed sources. This is a report of the reviewed record, not a medical examination or a claim that every condition has been ruled out.

Source and date: Nurse screening, September 8; teacher and OT consultation, September 10 | Documented findings: Vision screening passed at 20/20 each eye; hearing screening passed bilaterally under the school protocol. No reported uncorrected sensory concern. OT Jonah Reed, OTR/L, observed legible handwriting, functional pencil use, page tracking and classroom mobility; no motor barrier to the tested reading tasks was observed. Screening is not a diagnosis.

Source and date: Parent developmental/adaptive interview, September 11; teacher adaptive-function interview, September 14 | Documented findings: Developmental milestones reported within expected ranges, no regression. Independent dressing, meals, age-appropriate household routines and neighborhood safety routines; manages materials, follows multistep classroom routines, cooperates with peers and learns new nonreading routines. Reading homework requires help. These are descriptive interviews, not standardized adaptive scores; read with S5, not as an IQ substitute.

Source and date: School counselor review, September 15; teacher and parent reports; observations September 16 and 18 | Documented findings: No disciplinary removals; regular attendance and peer participation. Samira is frustrated and sometimes reluctant when asked to read aloud, but engaged in discussion, mathematics and supported science. Parent reports no pervasive mood/behavior change; counselor finds no cross-setting emotional pattern in the reviewed interviews/records. Reading errors occur when calm and attending, as well as when frustrated.

Source and date: Student interview, September 11 | Documented findings: Samira describes avoiding public reading because she loses her place while trying unfamiliar words, but likes telling stories and working with classmates. She requests private feedback. Her distress is acknowledged and supported; it is not treated as either proof or automatic exclusion of SLD.

evidenceSupplement.title: S7: Regular-classroom observation and relation to learning
evidenceSupplement.text:
On September 18, 9:05-9:40 a.m., Dr. Mercer observed Samira in the regular Grade 4 classroom during a science demonstration, independent reading and whole-class discussion; the evaluation observation followed August 24 parent consent. Melanie Voss taught the lesson in English using the class's ordinary demonstration, diagram and displayed vocabulary. The report records language, task difficulty and adult assistance separately.

Samira attended throughout the demonstration, answered 4/5 oral concept questions accurately and labeled 5/6 diagram parts from a word bank. During six minutes of independent reading of a new 180-word curriculum paragraph, she attempted 105 words, made 14 reading errors, and used first-letter guesses for 6 unfamiliar words. These are untimed classroom counts, not the timed fluency probes in S3. She paused, reread and requested two word pronunciations; subsequent assisted answers were not counted as independent reading. She explained the main science relationship accurately in discussion after the teacher reread the paragraph to the class.

In a separate 20-minute reading lesson observed that day, Samira explained a practiced decoding step after feedback and correctly read 8/10 taught words with prompts. The next-school-day independent probe on September 21 was 4/10; prompts and independent retention were not combined. This was a separate classroom word set, not the matched S8 probe sets. The observation links slow/error-prone decoding and limited independent carryover to reduced print access, while also documenting engagement, concept knowledge and helpful language supports.

evidenceSupplement.title: S8: Instructional comparison, retention, transfer and access
evidenceSupplement.text:
Nina Park's September 14-28 instructional review compared two matched, counterbalanced sets of familiar-vocabulary words with comparable taught spelling patterns. Across eight attended 25-minute sessions, each set received equal direct teaching time. Both conditions retained modeling, guided practice and correction; no needed support was withdrawn. General-intervention teaching used the existing small-group sequence and review schedule. Adapted teaching used steps selected from Samira's errors, fewer new contrasts at once, immediate error-specific feedback, spaced retrieval and planned application to new sentences. Sets were matched on spelling patterns and vocabulary familiarity; task differences and short duration limit causal inference. These are local descriptive probes, not a controlled experiment.

All probe values below are independently correct out of 10, without adult cues or supplied words. Matched focal sets were introduced September 14 and September 21; next-day probes occurred September 15 and September 22. Immediate checks used taught words; delayed checks used those words; transfer checks used new words with the same patterns. Subsequent sessions practiced the patterns with other words, without reteaching the focal words before their delayed checks. The September 28 probe tested week-2 focal words one week after introduction. Materials, exposure time and scoring rules were documented. Ordinary ESOL, vocabulary preview and access supports continued in both conditions.

Across September classroom assignments, audio/read-aloud plus visual vocabulary let Samira answer 8/10 content questions, versus 4/10 within the same work period reading independently. These access supports did not produce independent reading gains on new word probes (8/20 before and 9/20 after the review). Adapted instruction improved narrow-target independence and transfer, but did not eliminate the broader reading gap: mixed-word monitoring remained 9/20 and fluency 63 correct words/minute at 92% accuracy. The proposed ongoing instruction must therefore specify error-based sequencing, retrieval and transfer, with independent monitoring; a strategy name, staff title or setting alone does not establish necessity.

Rania reviewed the results September 28 with interpretation and supports continuing coordinated reading instruction and ESOL. Samira says the smaller steps help her know what to try and wants to use them without waiting for an adult. The short comparison supports instructional planning together with the long-term record; it is not proof that one branded program, fixed dosage or permanent placement is uniquely required.

evidenceSupplement.title: S9: Assessment-quality review and limits of the record
evidenceSupplement.text:
Dr. Mercer and Hana Nasser's September 30 review documents the question addressed by each method, language used, administration conditions, evaluator qualifications and limits. Standardized processing measures were administered in their published age range using required manual procedures; the score report was checked by a second qualified psychologist. Published reliability/validity evidence supports the selected constructs, but does not make every interpretation for every multilingual child valid. The team retained the processing results only for the bounded, corroborated purposes described in S5; it did not claim exact Arabic-English norm representativeness or use an improvised translated standard score.

Curriculum and monitoring probes used documented comparable difficulty, consistent instructions, independent scoring and repeated samples. Cross-source agreement is considered alongside variation across tasks and supports. ACCESS was administered by the trained ESOL teacher under the assessment's procedures; the 2026 reporting limits are retained. Family/student interviews and Arabic-language consultation add history and functional-language evidence but are not norm-referenced tests. Native-language information was actively obtained, while equivalent standardized Arabic achievement scores were not produced from limited Arabic literacy instruction or translated English tests.

Intentional omissions: secured test items, raw protocols, score confidence intervals, an FSIQ, a standardized adaptive scale, Arabic achievement equivalents and an unrelated medical battery are not supplied or required by this scenario. No significance tests, score conversions or diagnoses may be invented from their absence. The available sources provide the relevant evidence for the SLD-form exercise. Actual evaluations require professional judgment about additional suspected needs and applicable procedures; this training summary is not a universal battery or a legal compliance certification.

sections.title: Language, literacy, student and family evidence
paragraphs: Hana Nasser, Maine-certified ESOL teacher, and Dalia Mansour, qualified Arabic-English language consultant, interviewed Samira and Rania on September 11. Samira has heard and used Levantine Arabic from birth and English since preschool at age 4. She has attended this English-medium school continuously since kindergarten in fall 2022. Arabic and English are both used at home; the family describes detailed, sequenced Arabic stories and age-appropriate everyday conversations. A 45-minute weekly community class since September 2024 provides introductory Modern Standard Arabic print instruction. Samira reads some taught Arabic words, but this exposure is not equivalent to her English literacy instruction; no Arabic-English reading-score comparison is made.

The simulated February 2026 Grade 3 ACCESS Online report gives the domain proficiency-level scores below. These are English-proficiency results, not disability or achievement scores. WIDA's 2025-2026 reset means scale scores cannot be compared with prior years; the 2026 proficiency-level scores also require caution because they use the prior cut scores. No overall score is computed here. The team uses the snapshot with classroom evidence, not as an exit rule or a waiting period for evaluation.

Comparable oral-language samples with familiar content, pictures and the same 0-12 local rubric improved from 7/12 in September 2025 to 10/12 in September 2026: more complete explanations, causal vocabulary and clarification of misunderstandings. In September Samira correctly explained 18/20 familiar spoken word meanings but independently read only 9/20 different printed words using the same taught spelling patterns. Directions and vocabulary were checked before local decoding tasks. The word-reading errors persisted on familiar English vocabulary, including sounds shared across her languages; neither this check nor bilingual status by itself identifies a disability.

Rania reports stable housing, food access, predictable caregiving and regular access to school materials, with no schooling interruption or chronic disruption during the reviewed period. She values Arabic use and wants interpreted progress updates. Samira wants to read her science-display captions independently. The school does not treat family income, language, culture or limited formal Arabic literacy as an explanation without evidence.

sections.title: Appropriate instruction, delivery and repeated progress
paragraphs: Teacher/interventionist records reviewed September 28 document qualified, Maine-certified teachers, 97% attendance across the reviewed school period, and daily 90-minute English literacy instruction. Core teaching included explicit phonemic analysis, cumulative phonics/word analysis, spelling, supported oral reading, vocabulary and comprehension, with modeling, guided practice and correction. ESOL was 30 minutes four days weekly; visual directions, clarified vocabulary, oral rehearsal and content-language support were available daily. These methods addressed the English literacy skills assessed here; attendance alone was not used to establish instructional adequacy.

Reading specialist Nina Park delivered a research-based explicit decoding/fluency intervention in addition to core instruction. The methods used sound-letter analysis, word-part decoding and supported connected-text reading, drawing on the WWC foundational-skills and Grades 4-9 intervention guides listed below; this does not imply that the fictional local program itself has been validated. Four 25-minute sessions were planned weekly across nine instructional weeks April 6-June 12 (excluding spring break) and five instructional weeks August 24-September 25. Of 56 planned sessions, 51 occurred: 34/36 in spring and 17/20 in fall. Two absences and three school-event cancellations account for five missed sessions. No school intervention was delivered during summer; voluntary home materials were not counted as sessions. These are 14 instructional weeks, not 14 uninterrupted calendar weeks.

Checks by the literacy coach on April 17, May 15, August 28 and September 18 documented respectively 9/10, 10/10, 9/10 and 10/10 planned lesson elements: explicit modeling, guided practice, immediate feedback and cumulative review. Hana verified access to directions and task vocabulary at each review. The last two weeks included the instructional comparison in S8. The broad monitoring probes below remained independent, unpracticed and at the same difficulty; narrow taught-item gains in S8 do not replace them.

At each review date below, Rania received the results and explanation through a qualified Arabic interpreter. Review notes recorded her questions and the next instructional adjustment. The word-list and fluency data were not withheld until the eligibility meeting.

sections.title: Regular-classroom observation and relation to learning
paragraphs: On September 18, 9:05-9:40 a.m., Dr. Mercer observed Samira in the regular Grade 4 classroom during a science demonstration, independent reading and whole-class discussion; the evaluation observation followed August 24 parent consent. Melanie Voss taught the lesson in English using the class's ordinary demonstration, diagram and displayed vocabulary. The report records language, task difficulty and adult assistance separately.

Samira attended throughout the demonstration, answered 4/5 oral concept questions accurately and labeled 5/6 diagram parts from a word bank. During six minutes of independent reading of a new 180-word curriculum paragraph, she attempted 105 words, made 14 reading errors, and used first-letter guesses for 6 unfamiliar words. These are untimed classroom counts, not the timed fluency probes in S3. She paused, reread and requested two word pronunciations; subsequent assisted answers were not counted as independent reading. She explained the main science relationship accurately in discussion after the teacher reread the paragraph to the class.

In a separate 20-minute reading lesson observed that day, Samira explained a practiced decoding step after feedback and correctly read 8/10 taught words with prompts. The next-school-day independent probe on September 21 was 4/10; prompts and independent retention were not combined. This was a separate classroom word set, not the matched S8 probe sets. The observation links slow/error-prone decoding and limited independent carryover to reduced print access, while also documenting engagement, concept knowledge and helpful language supports.

sections.title: Instructional comparison, retention, transfer and access
paragraphs: Nina Park's September 14-28 instructional review compared two matched, counterbalanced sets of familiar-vocabulary words with comparable taught spelling patterns. Across eight attended 25-minute sessions, each set received equal direct teaching time. Both conditions retained modeling, guided practice and correction; no needed support was withdrawn. General-intervention teaching used the existing small-group sequence and review schedule. Adapted teaching used steps selected from Samira's errors, fewer new contrasts at once, immediate error-specific feedback, spaced retrieval and planned application to new sentences. Sets were matched on spelling patterns and vocabulary familiarity; task differences and short duration limit causal inference. These are local descriptive probes, not a controlled experiment.

All probe values below are independently correct out of 10, without adult cues or supplied words. Matched focal sets were introduced September 14 and September 21; next-day probes occurred September 15 and September 22. Immediate checks used taught words; delayed checks used those words; transfer checks used new words with the same patterns. Subsequent sessions practiced the patterns with other words, without reteaching the focal words before their delayed checks. The September 28 probe tested week-2 focal words one week after introduction. Materials, exposure time and scoring rules were documented. Ordinary ESOL, vocabulary preview and access supports continued in both conditions.

Across September classroom assignments, audio/read-aloud plus visual vocabulary let Samira answer 8/10 content questions, versus 4/10 within the same work period reading independently. These access supports did not produce independent reading gains on new word probes (8/20 before and 9/20 after the review). Adapted instruction improved narrow-target independence and transfer, but did not eliminate the broader reading gap: mixed-word monitoring remained 9/20 and fluency 63 correct words/minute at 92% accuracy. The proposed ongoing instruction must therefore specify error-based sequencing, retrieval and transfer, with independent monitoring; a strategy name, staff title or setting alone does not establish necessity.

Rania reviewed the results September 28 with interpretation and supports continuing coordinated reading instruction and ESOL. Samira says the smaller steps help her know what to try and wants to use them without waiting for an adult. The short comparison supports instructional planning together with the long-term record; it is not proof that one branded program, fixed dosage or permanent placement is uniquely required.

narrative: Samira is age 9 years, 8 months, in Grade 4. She uses Arabic and English with family and friends and has attended the same English-medium school since kindergarten, with 97% attendance. The amount and type of literacy instruction differ across the two languages; Arabic reading is not treated as a second equivalent test of English reading.

Samira enjoys making illustrated explanations and discussing science investigations. In English she increasingly explains familiar content with precise vocabulary when visuals and planning time are available. Unfamiliar-word reading and connected-text fluency remain difficult despite verified explicit reading instruction, language access and targeted intervention. The comprehensive evaluation reviews all eight academic areas and establishes inadequate basic reading and reading fluency for age and Grade 4 expectations using appropriate performance evidence.

The fictional full evaluation combines longitudinal work, classroom observations, intervention response, language-development evidence, appropriate achievement and psychological-processing assessment, and student/family input. cases.title: Avery, Grade 6: mathematics and a school transition
cases.practiceFocus: Mathematics evidence, continuity of instruction and generalization
cases.languageContext: English used at home and school; evaluation language and access appropriate for this fictional learner
narrative: Avery is age 11 years, 6 months, in Grade 6 and moved to a new school at the beginning of Grade 5. Avery enjoys building stage sets and explaining how shapes fit together. The family describes strong reading interests and difficulty completing calculations without losing track of place value. Attendance is 96%. Earlier records show similar mathematics concerns before the move; a transition is part of the history, not an assumed explanation for disability or underachievement.

The comprehensive evaluation reviews all eight academic areas. Appropriate age-based measures and independent grade-level work establish inadequate mathematics calculation and mathematics problem-solving, with stronger reading, language and visual representation skills. The full team review documents a relevant pattern across intervention response, classroom performance, achievement and appropriate psychological-processing evidence. For this exercise, that review establishes SLD in mathematics. The short score excerpt does not independently establish those findings.

Records from both schools verify appropriate mathematics instruction by qualified staff, including the prerequisite skills relevant to the current errors. The team reviews health/sensory information, developmental history, language access, emotional functioning and family/context evidence and finds no listed Q3 factor to be the primary cause. No educationally relevant medical finding is reported. The original evaluation's validity and qualifications are stipulated as established.

Avery can represent a problem with a drawing but often misaligns place value, loses regrouping steps and chooses an operation without checking the relationships in the problem. Extra time does not consistently resolve the errors. An intervention with worked examples, concrete-to-symbolic links and guided self-explanation improves performance on practiced tasks. The current excerpt does not establish whether general education adequately meets the need or which disability-related adaptations are necessary for independent transfer. The Q9 decision therefore remains open.

evidenceSupplement.title: Observed: calculation, reasoning and supports

In a follow-up task, reading the directions aloud does not remove the errors. A calculator improves arithmetic accuracy but does not reliably improve operation selection. Teacher prompts improve completion, but prompted answers are recorded separately from independent work. These observations distinguish possible instructional targets without making one support a diagnostic test.

evidenceSupplement.title: Documented in the fictional log: improvement and limits
evidenceSupplement.text: The intervention record shows 27 of 30 planned 30-minute lessons over ten weeks; the three cancellations are documented. Three fidelity observations show the planned models, worked examples and self-explanation routine. On equivalent ten-problem checks of taught calculation skills, independent accuracy rises from 4 to 8. On unpracticed application problems it rises from 3 to 5. Checks use new problems with matched task demands. Counts are classroom evidence, not standardized scores, and the record does not isolate which teaching component produced the change.

Family reports that homework improves with a worked example beside it but new formats remain difficult. Before selecting Q9a or Q9b, the team needs to describe the instruction actually required, review maintenance and transfer, and determine general education sufficiency. Do not delay required evaluation procedures or withdraw needed support to manufacture this comparison.

debrief.purpose: Compare participants' reasoning after they explain their selections. No automatic evidence grade or real eligibility verdict.
alexCalibration: Reading Comprehension 94 is relatively stronger. Reconcile task demands, reading rate, supports and classroom work; it does not alone establish Grade 4 mastery.
Basic Reading, Decoding and Phonological Processing reuse subtests. Shared subtests do not become independent confirmation merely because they appear in several composites.
Processing Speed 86 or an IQ-achievement difference alone does not settle Q8 or Q9. Spelling 87 needs writing-sample evidence.
Different supported evidence selections are acceptable. Ask which independent sources support the concern and what evidence could change the recommendation.
facilitatorPrompts: What evidence establishes general education sufficiency?
Which teaching adaptation is necessary, and why?
What information could change or complete the recommendation?

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Q2 is YES because underachievement is due to inadequate instruction. Which question comes next?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Q8. A Q2 YES response directs the team to Q8/no SLD qualification. Continue appropriate instruction, support and evaluation of other suspected needs as warranted.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A child has anxiety and reading difficulty. What must Q3 determine?
options: Whether reading scores fall below a fixed cutoff
Whether an exclusionary factor primarily explains the underachievement
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Analyze primary cause. The coexistence of anxiety and reading difficulty does not by itself establish the cause of the underachievement or resolve the SLD question.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Q8 is YES. General education adequately meets the need. Which Q9 option fits?
options: 9b: general education adequately meets the need
Q8 must automatically change to NO
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Q9b. The stated general education sufficiency does not support special-education eligibility under SLD, even if Q8 remains YES. Section 504 is a separate determination. Progress alone does not remove SDI need when progress depends on SDI.
